items.title: Digital Twin Technology in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
items.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is an emerging digital technogy that is gaining importance in modern pharmaceutical manufacturing. It creates a virtual representation of a physical machine, process, product, or manufacturing facility and connects it with real-time information from the actual system. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, data from sensors, manufacturing equipment, and Process Analytical Technology (PAT) can be combined with mathematical, statistical, mechan istic, and data-driven models to understand how a process behaves. This helps manufacturers monitor processes continuously, identify changes at an early stage, and maintain consistent product quality. Digital Twin technology can be used in different pharmaceutical operations such as mixing, granulation, drying, tablet compression, coating, filling, and packaging. It also has potential applications in biopharmaceutical processes such as cell culture, fermentation, filtration, and purification. One of the major benefits of a digital twin is that it allows manufacturers to observe and analyze a process without depending only on physical testing. It can also be used to study different process conditions virtually before making changes to the actual manufacturing process. This may help in process optimization and reduce unnecessary experiments. Digital twins can support Quality by Design (QbD) by improving the understanding of the relationship between raw materials, process parameters, and critical quality attributes. They are also useful in continuous manufacturing, where large amounts of real-time process data are generated. Another important application is predictive maintenance, where equipment data can be analyzed to identify unusual changes and possible equipment failures before they occur. When digital twins are combined with PAT, artificial intelligence, machine learning, Internet of Things (IoT), and cloud computing, they can provide more detailed information about pharmaceutical processes and support the development of Pharma 4.0. Digital twins may also support real-time release testing, process optimization, manufacturing simulation, and predictive quality management. However, several challenges need to be considered before their widespread use. These include data quality, data integrity, model accuracy, system interoperability, cybersecurity, high implementation costs, model validation, and regulatory requirements. Pharmaceutical manufacturing also requires strict control and documentation, so digital-twin models used for important manufacturing or quality decisions need to be properly validated and maintained. In addition, successful implementation requires cooperation between pharmaceutical scientists, engineers, data scientists, IT professionals, and quality-control teams. Human involvement is still important because professionals need to understand the information provided by the digital twin and make appropriate decisions. Although digital twin technology is still developing, it has considerable potential to improve pharmaceutical manufacturing by supporting better process understanding, real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, process optimization, and quality management. Future developments are expected to focus on better integration with artificial intelligence, continuous manufacturing, advanced analytical technologies, and automated manufacturing systems. Overall, Digital Twin technology can play an important role in the digital transformation of pharmaceutical manufacturing and may contribute to more efficient, consistent, flexible, and data-driven production.[1-5]

items.title: Digital-Age Ethics for Elementary Teachers: Challenges and Strategies for Professional Integrity
items.abstract: Digital transformation has expanded elementary teachers’ work into learning platforms, social media, messaging applications, data systems, and generative artificial intelligence. These tools support collaboration and instructional improvement but raise ethical concerns about professional boundaries, children’s privacy and safety, information integrity, copyright, equity, and accountability. This article synthesizes the ethical challenges faced by elementary school teachers in digital environments and identifies strategies for maintaining professional integrity while prioritizing children’s best interests. A narrative literature review was conducted through exploratory searches of scholarly articles, academic books, international frameworks, policy documents, and Indonesian legislation, prioritizing publications from 2020 to 2026 alongside foundational theories. The thematic synthesis identifies risks involving blurred personal and professional boundaries, children’s data governance, unsafe online communication, unverified digital and AI-generated content, and unequal access to technology. It proposes a Five-Dimension Framework of Teachers’ Digital Integrity comprising pedagogical, relational, information-and-data, epistemic, and civic-professional integrity. Recommendations are directed to teachers, schools, teacher education programs, families, and professional associations. The framework is a conceptual synthesis, not a validated instrument, and requires empirical testing in Indonesian elementary schools
